'''''Clematis vitalba''''' (also known as '''old man's beard'''<ref name=Proudley>{{cite book |author1=Brian Proudley |author2=Valerie Proudley |title=Heathers in Colour |date=1989 |publisher=Blandford Press |isbn=0713714204 |page=37 |edition=2nd |quote=The sort of plants already growing on the site will give a clue as to the nature of the soil. ... The presence of Old Man's Beard (''Clematis vitalba''), Beech (''Fagus sylvatica'') and Yew (''Taxus baccata'') are likely to mean that lime is present.}}</ref> and '''traveller's joy''') is a shrub in the genus ''Clematis'' of the family [[Ranunculaceae]]. It is native to Europe and western Asia.

==Description==
''Clematis vitalba'' is a climbing shrub with branched, grooved [[Plant stem|stem]]s, [[deciduous]] leaves, and scented greeny-white flowers with fluffy underlying [[sepal]]s. The many fruits formed in each [[inflorescence]] have long silky appendages which, seen together, give the characteristic appearance of ''old man's beard''. The grooves along the stems of ''C. vitalba'' can easily be felt when handling the plant.{{citation needed|date=March 2026}}

This species is eaten by the [[larva]]e of a wide range of [[moth]]s. This includes many species which are reliant on it as their sole foodplant; including [[small emerald]], [[small waved umber]] and [[Haworth's pug]].{{citation needed|date=March 2026}}

==Range==
''C. vitalba'' has a preference for base rich alkaline soils and moist climate with warm summers.{{citation needed|date=October 2022}} The species is native to [[Eurasia]] and [[North Africa]].<ref name=burke>{{cite web |title=Clematis vitalba |url=https://biology.burke.washington.edu/herbarium/imagecollection/taxon.php?Taxon=Clematis%20vitalba |website=biology.burke.washington.edu |access-date=10 October 2022}}</ref>

===United Kingdom===
In the UK it is a native plant and is common throughout England south of a line between the [[River Mersey]] and the [[River Humber]]. It also commonly occurs in southern, eastern and northern Wales. Outside of these areas it is widely planted and occurs as far north as the southern highlands of Scotland.<ref>New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora</ref>

===As an invasive species===
Due to its disseminators reproductive system, vitality, and climbing behavior, ''Clematis vitalba'' is an invasive plant in many places.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Clematis vitalba Profile – California Invasive Plant Council |url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/profile/clematis-vitalba-profile/ |access-date=2024-01-22 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Invasive Species Compendium |title=Clematis vitalba |url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/?compid=5&dsid=14280&loadmodule=datasheet&page=481&site=144 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120401141920/http://www.cabi.org/isc/?compid=5&dsid=14280&loadmodule=datasheet&page=481&site=144 |archive-date=2012-04-01 |accessdate=2017-05-24}}</ref> The species is capable of rapid growth, climbing several times faster than [[English ivy]], and each plant may produce in excess of 100,000 seeds. The plant may also spread through stem and root fragmentation.<ref name=pbes>{{cite web |title=Old Man's Beard (Clematis vitalba) |url=https://www.portlandoregon.gov/bes/article/172621 |website=portland.gov |publisher=Portland Bureau of Environmental Services |access-date=10 October 2022}}</ref>

====New Zealand====
{{Main|Old man's beard in New Zealand}}
In [[New Zealand]] it is declared an "unwanted organism" and is listed in the [[National Pest Plant Accord]]. It cannot be sold, propagated or distributed.  It is a potential threat to native plants since it grows vigorously and forms a canopy which smothers other plants and has no natural controlling organisms in New Zealand. Species of ''Clematis'' native to New Zealand have smooth stems and can easily be differentiated from ''C. vitalba'' by touch.{{citation needed|date=October 2022}}

====North America====
In [[North America]], old man's beard is considered an invasive species. It is found in Washington, Oregon, California, and British Columbia. The species is also found in the [[eastern United States]].<ref name=burke/> The species was introduced as an ornamental plant in the [[Pacific Northwest]] sometime between 1950 and 1970.<ref name=pbes/>

==Names==

The name "traveller's joy" was given to the plant by herbalist [[John Gerard]], who wrote in his 1597 ''Herball'' that he gave it that name because the plant was found "adorning waies and hedges where people travel".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Evans |first=Paul |date=January 28, 2015 |title=Social climber with a crusty bark |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2015/jan/28/country-diary-evans-wenlock-edge-travellers-joy-clematis |website=The Guardian }}</ref> The plant is also known as wild clematis, old man’s beard, shepherd’s delight and smokewood.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chester |first=Nicola |date=January 4, 2020 |title=Country diary: wild clematis in winter is a magical plant |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/jan/04/country-diary-wild-clematis-in-winter-is-a-magical-plant |website=The Guardian }}</ref>

==Characteristics==
*Reproductive organs:
** Inflorescence type: [[Parity (medicine)|biparous]] [[Inflorescence#Organization|cyme]]
** Sex:  [[hermaphrodite]]
** Type of pollination:  [[entomophily|entomophilous]]
*Seed:
** Type of fruit:  [[achene]]
** Dissemination:  With the wind
*Habitat and distribution:
** Type of habitat: [[Central Europe|Mid-European]] shrubberies, mountainsides, in moderately [[eutrophic]] regions
** Distribution: [[Holarctic]]

''C. vitalba'' grows well in [[agricultural lime|limey]] soils.<ref name=Proudley />

==Diseases==
''C. vitalba'' suffers from ''[[tomato spotted wilt virus]]''.<ref name="TSWV-EPPO">{{cite web | title=''Tomato spotted wilt virus'' (TSWV00){{bracket|Overview}} | website=Global Database | publisher=EPPO ([[European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization]]) | date=2002-11-26 | url=http://gd.eppo.int/taxon/TSWV00 | access-date=2022-05-05}}</ref>

==Use==
''Clematis vitalba'' was used to make rope during the Stone Age in Switzerland.<ref>Johnson, Magnus. 2001. ''The genus Clematis.'' Södertälje: Magnus Johnsons Plantskola AB, p. 37.</ref> In Slovenia, the stems of the plant were used for binding crops and weaving baskets for onions.<ref>Petauer, Tomaž. 1993. ''Leksikon rastlinskih bogastev''. Ljubljana: Tehniška založba Slovenije, p. 139.</ref> It was particularly useful for binding sheaves of grain because mice do not gnaw on it.<ref>[http://www.zaveza.si/index.php/revija-zaveza/100-zaveza-t-42 Kržan, Vanja. 2010. "Mi pa oznanjamo Kristusa, križanega (1 Kor 1,23)." ''Zaveza'' 42 (25 February).] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120629012543/http://www.zaveza.si/index.php/revija-zaveza/100-zaveza-t-42 |date=2012-06-29 }} {{in lang|sl}}</ref> In [[Italy]], the sprouts are harvested to make omelettes (called "vitalbini" in [[Tuscany]], "visoni" in [[Veneto]]).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://tessyoungdesigns.com/2020/07/14/vitalbini/ |title=Vitalbini |last=Young |first=Tess |date=2020-07-14 |website=Tess Young Designs and Makes |publisher=Tess Young |access-date=2025-01-06 |quote=}}</ref>
